TOP SECRET

October 16 to 28, 1962

Thirteen Days in October

The Cuban Missile Crisis

An American spy plane has photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites being built in Cuba, just 90 miles from Florida. Every decision you make in the next thirteen days could start a nuclear war or prevent one.

The White House, April 18, 1961

The Bay of Pigs

You have been President for less than three months. Before you took office, the CIA trained about 1,400 Cuban exiles to invade Cuba and overthrow Fidel Castro. You approved the plan on one condition: no one can know the United States is behind it.

Yesterday the exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs on Cuba’s southern coast. It is going badly. Castro’s planes sank two of their supply ships, and thousands of Cuban troops are closing in. The exiles are trapped on the beach and running out of ammunition.

American jets on the aircraft carrier USS Essex, waiting off the coast, could still save the invasion. But if American planes attack Cuba, the whole world will know the United States planned it.

Will you send American jets to support the invasion?

April 1961

You sent in the jets

Incorrect

Kennedy refused to let American jets attack Cuba. He was determined to keep the United States’ role in the invasion hidden.

The outcome of this choice will go here.

April 1961

You kept the United States out of it

Correct

Kennedy refused to let American jets attack Cuba. He was determined to keep the United States’ role in the invasion hidden.

The White House, 1961

Missiles in Europe

Before you took office, the United States promised its NATO allies a new weapon: the Jupiter, a nuclear missile that can travel about 1,500 miles. Now it is your job to decide where the Jupiters will go.

To threaten the Soviet Union, the missiles must be close enough to reach it. They can only be placed in a NATO country that agrees to host them.

Click two NATO countries, then place the missiles.

NATO (can be selected) Soviet Union and Warsaw Pact Neutral or non-NATO Your choice

Missile sites: none chosen

1961 to 1962

You placed the missiles

The real Jupiter missiles went to Italy and Turkey: 30 in Italy and 15 in Turkey. Turkey borders the Soviet Union, and missiles there could reach Moscow. Soviet leaders saw them as a direct threat.

Havana, May 1962

An Offer from Moscow

You are now Fidel Castro. One year ago, your forces crushed the American-backed invasion at the Bay of Pigs. But the United States has not given up. The CIA is plotting to overthrow you, the Americans have cut off trade with Cuba, and the U.S. military is practicing invasions of Caribbean islands.

Now Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev has sent a delegation to Havana with a secret offer: the Soviet Union will place nuclear missiles in Cuba. Khrushchev says the missiles will stop the Americans from ever invading again, and they will answer the American missiles in Italy and Turkey.

But if the Americans discover the missiles before they are ready, Cuba could become the first target in a nuclear war.

Will you accept the Soviet missiles?

Summer 1962

You accepted the missiles

Correct

Castro accepted the Soviet offer. That summer, the Soviet Union secretly began shipping nuclear missiles and about 40,000 soldiers to Cuba.

Summer 1962

Incorrect

The White House, October 16, 1962

The Missiles Are Discovered

You are President Kennedy again. This morning, your national security adviser brought you photographs taken two days ago by a U-2 spy plane flying over western Cuba. The CIA has studied them closely. They show Soviet SS-4 medium-range ballistic missiles.

An SS-4 can carry a nuclear warhead about 1,200 miles, far enough to hit Washington, D.C. The Soviets have promised you there are no offensive weapons in Cuba.

Now you are meeting with the ExComm, your closest advisers. The Soviets do not know you have found the missiles, and the sites are not ready to fire yet. Nobody in the room agrees yet on how to respond.

Will you keep the missiles secret or tell the American people?

October 16 to 22, 1962

You kept it secret

Correct

Kennedy kept the discovery secret for six days. He stuck to his normal schedule so no one would grow suspicious while the ExComm debated what to do. He finally told the nation in a televised speech on October 22.

The outcome of this choice will go here.

October 16 to 22, 1962

You told the public

Incorrect

Kennedy kept the discovery secret for six days. He stuck to his normal schedule so no one would grow suspicious while the ExComm debated what to do. He finally told the nation in a televised speech on October 22.

The Oval Office, October 18, 1962

A Visit from Gromyko

Two days have passed since you learned about the missiles. The ExComm is still debating what to do, and the Soviets still do not know you have found them.

This afternoon, Soviet Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko is sitting across from you in the Oval Office. He tells you that Soviet aid to Cuba is only meant to help Cuba defend itself, and that the Soviet Union would never send offensive weapons there. You have seen the photographs. You know he is not telling the truth.

If you confront him now, the Soviets will know their secret is out. If you stay quiet, you keep that advantage, but you let the lie stand.

Will you confront Gromyko with the photographs?

October 18, 1962

You confronted Gromyko

Incorrect

Kennedy said nothing about the photographs. He reminded Gromyko of his earlier public warning against putting offensive weapons in Cuba, but he let the Soviets go on believing their secret was safe until his speech on October 22.

The outcome of this choice will go here.

October 18, 1962

You kept the secret

Correct

Kennedy said nothing about the photographs. He reminded Gromyko of his earlier public warning against putting offensive weapons in Cuba, but he let the Soviets go on believing their secret was safe until his speech on October 22.

The White House, October 21, 1962

Four Options

Five days have passed since the missiles were discovered. New U-2 photos show Soviet crews working around the clock. The planes have also found sites for even larger missiles that could reach almost every city in the United States. Some of the missiles could be ready to fire within days.

Your advisers have argued all week. The Joint Chiefs of Staff want to attack. Others warn that an attack could start a nuclear war. The ExComm has narrowed your choices to four options, and tomorrow night you will tell the nation what you have decided.

How will you respond to the missiles in Cuba?

October 22, 1962

You chose diplomacy

Incorrect

Kennedy chose a naval blockade. He called it a “quarantine,” because a blockade is legally an act of war, and he announced it to the nation on October 22. Many of his military advisers wanted air strikes or an invasion. Decades later, Americans learned that Soviet forces in Cuba had short-range nuclear weapons that could have been used against invading troops.

The White House, October 22, 1962

Choosing the Words

Tonight at 7 p.m., you will go on television and tell the American people about the missiles in Cuba. Millions of people around the world will be listening, including Nikita Khrushchev.

You have chosen a naval blockade. American warships will stop ships headed for Cuba, search them, and turn back any that carry weapons. But there is a problem: under international law, a blockade is an act of war. If you announce a “blockade,” the Soviets could say the United States started a war and answer with force.

Your speech needs a different name for what the Navy is about to do.

What will you call the naval blockade in your speech?

October 22, 1962

You called it a blockade

Incorrect

Kennedy called it a “quarantine.” The word made the action sound defensive, like stopping a dangerous disease from spreading, rather than an act of war. The quarantine only stopped offensive weapons, so ships carrying food and other everyday goods could still reach Cuba.

The outcome of this choice will go here.

October 22, 1962

You called it a quarantine

Correct

Kennedy called it a “quarantine.” The word made the action sound defensive, like stopping a dangerous disease from spreading, rather than an act of war. The quarantine only stopped offensive weapons, so ships carrying food and other everyday goods could still reach Cuba.

Soviet submarine B-59, in the Atlantic near Cuba, October 27, 1962

Under the Sea

You are now Vasili Arkhipov, a senior officer aboard the Soviet submarine B-59. Hidden on board is a torpedo with a nuclear warhead, about as powerful as the bomb dropped on Hiroshima.

Today, American destroyers have trapped B-59 underwater. They are dropping explosives that slam against the hull. The Americans mean them only as a signal to come up, but nobody aboard knows that. Inside, the heat is unbearable, the air is running out, and the batteries are nearly dead. You have not heard from Moscow in days, and you do not know if the war has already started.

Captain Valentin Savitsky believes it has. He orders the nuclear torpedo made ready to fire. Launching it requires three officers to agree: the captain, the political officer, and you. The other two are ready. Everything depends on you.

Will you agree to launch the nuclear torpedo?

October 27, 1962

You agreed to launch the torpedo

Incorrect

Arkhipov refused. He calmed Captain Savitsky and convinced him to bring B-59 to the surface. Surrounded by American warships, the submarine turned around and headed home. If the torpedo had been fired, it could have destroyed an American ship and set off a nuclear war. The world did not learn the full story until 2002, when former crew members described what happened, and Arkhipov is now often called the man who saved the world.

The outcome of this choice will go here.

October 27, 1962

You refused to launch

Correct

Arkhipov refused. He calmed Captain Savitsky and convinced him to bring B-59 to the surface. Surrounded by American warships, the submarine turned around and headed home. If the torpedo had been fired, it could have destroyed an American ship and set off a nuclear war. The Kremlin, Moscow, October 26, 1962

Making a Deal

You are now Nikita Khrushchev, leader of the Soviet Union. Kennedy’s quarantine has stopped your ships at sea, and the Americans have shown photographs of your missiles to the entire world at the United Nations.

American nuclear bombers are in the air around the clock, and U.S. troops are gathering in Florida for a possible invasion of Cuba. Your missiles are almost ready, but a war with the United States could destroy your country.

You decide to write to Kennedy and offer a deal. You will remove your missiles from Cuba, but you want something in return.

Choose two demands to include in your proposal.

Your demands: none chosen

October 26 to 28, 1962

Your proposal to Kennedy

Khrushchev’s first letter asked Kennedy to promise not to invade Cuba. A second letter added a new demand: remove the American missiles from Turkey. Kennedy publicly promised not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove the missiles from Turkey. In return, the Soviet Union took its missiles out of Cuba.

The outcome of this choice will go here.

The Justice Department, Washington, October 27, 1962

A Secret Meeting

You are now Robert Kennedy, the Attorney General of the United States and the President’s younger brother. Today has been the most dangerous day of the crisis. This morning, Khrushchev sent a second letter demanding that the United States remove its missiles from Turkey. This afternoon, a Soviet missile shot down an American U-2 over Cuba, killing the pilot, Major Rudolf Anderson. The military is pressing the President to attack.

This evening, the President answered Khrushchev’s first letter and released his reply to the public. In it, he agreed that if the Soviets remove their missiles from Cuba, the United States will promise not to invade Cuba. Khrushchev has not answered.

Now your brother has sent you to meet privately with Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin, and Dobrynin wants to know about the missiles in Turkey. Turkey is a NATO ally. Giving up its missiles in public would look like America abandoning a friend because the Soviets made threats. But without a deal, Khrushchev may refuse to back down.

Will you agree to remove the Jupiter missiles from Turkey?

October 27 to 28, 1962

You agreed to remove the missiles

Correct

Robert Kennedy told Dobrynin that the United States could not make a public deal about Turkey, but that the Jupiter missiles would be gone within four to five months, as long as the Soviets kept that part of the deal secret. The next morning, Khrushchev announced that the Soviet missiles would leave Cuba. The Jupiters were quietly removed from Turkey in April 1963, and the secret deal stayed hidden from the public for years.

The outcome of this choice will go here.

October 27 to 28, 1962

You kept the missiles in Turkey

Incorrect

Robert Kennedy told Dobrynin that the United States could not make a public deal about Turkey, but that the Jupiter missiles would be gone within four to five months, as long as the Soviets kept that part of the deal secret. Havana, October 28, 1962

Left Out of the Deal

You are Fidel Castro again. This morning, Khrushchev announced on Moscow radio that the Soviet missiles will be taken out of Cuba. In return, Kennedy has promised not to invade. You learned about it from the news, just like everyone else.

Khrushchev never asked your opinion. The future of your country was decided in Washington and Moscow, and Cuba had no say. You are furious.

Kennedy’s promise is only words, and you do not trust the Americans to keep it. If Cuba is going to accept this deal, you want real guarantees. You will announce your own conditions to the world.

Choose the five demands the United States must meet.

Your demands: 0 of 5 chosen

October 28, 1962

Castro’s five demands

Castro demanded that the United States end its trade embargo, stop its sabotage and spying against Cuba, stop the raids by Cuban exiles, keep its spy planes and warships out of Cuban territory, and leave Guantánamo Bay. The United States ignored all five, and the Soviets did not push for any of them. Castro struck back by refusing to let United Nations inspectors into Cuba to confirm the missiles were gone.

November 1962 to August 1963

Aftermath

The Soviet missiles were leaving Cuba, but the crisis was not quite over. Over the next ten months, the United States and the Soviet Union settled the last arguments, kept their secret deal, and built new ways to keep a crisis like this from happening again.

  1. Late October to November 1962

    Castro blocks the inspectors

    The deal called for United Nations inspectors to confirm the missiles were gone. When UN Secretary-General U Thant flew to Havana, Castro refused to let any inspectors into Cuba. He would not let the superpowers decide Cuba’s future a second time.

  2. Early November 1962

    Missiles on deck

    With no inspectors allowed, the Soviets shipped their missiles home on the open decks of their cargo ships. American planes and warships pulled alongside, and Soviet crews pulled back the covers so the Americans could photograph and count all 42 missiles.

  3. November 2 to 26, 1962

    Moscow tries to calm Castro

    Soviet Deputy Premier Anastas Mikoyan spent more than three weeks in Havana trying to repair the friendship with an angry Castro. Castro asked to keep the Soviets’ short-range nuclear weapons, which the Americans did not know were in Cuba. Mikoyan refused, and every Soviet nuclear warhead left Cuba by December.

  4. November 20, 1962

    The quarantine ends

    One last argument remained. Kennedy insisted that Soviet IL-28 bombers in Cuba were offensive weapons that also had to go. Khrushchev agreed to remove them, and that evening Kennedy announced that the quarantine was over. American forces began standing down from their highest alert.

  5. November 1962

    A promise never signed

    Because Castro would not allow inspections, the United States never put its promise not to invade Cuba into a formal written agreement. Even so, the United States never invaded, and Castro stayed in power for more than 45 years.

  6. December 1962

    The Bay of Pigs prisoners come home

    Cuba had held more than 1,100 members of the invasion force since April 1961. Castro released them in exchange for about $53 million in food and medicine. On December 29, Kennedy welcomed the freed prisoners at a ceremony in Miami’s Orange Bowl.

  7. January 7, 1963

    The crisis officially closes

    The United States and the Soviet Union sent a joint letter to the United Nations saying they no longer needed the Security Council to deal with the crisis.

  8. April 1963

    The Jupiters leave Turkey

    The United States kept its secret promise. The Jupiter missiles were removed from Turkey and Italy, and American submarines carrying Polaris nuclear missiles began patrolling the Mediterranean instead. The public would not learn about the trade for years.

  9. April to June 1963

    Castro visits the Soviet Union

    Khrushchev invited Castro on a tour of the Soviet Union that lasted more than a month. Huge crowds greeted him, and the visit helped heal the anger left over from October.

  10. June 10, 1963

    A strategy of peace

    In a speech at American University in Washington, Kennedy asked Americans to rethink the Cold War and to remember that Americans and Soviets shared the same small planet. He announced new talks to limit nuclear testing.

  11. June 20, 1963

    The hotline agreement

    During the crisis, messages between Kennedy and Khrushchev took hours to deliver and translate. Khrushchev even announced his final decision over Moscow radio because it was faster than official channels. In Geneva, the two countries signed an agreement to create a direct communication link between Washington and Moscow.

  12. August 5, 1963

    The Limited Test Ban Treaty

    The United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain agreed to stop testing nuclear weapons in the atmosphere, in outer space, and underwater. It was the first major agreement to limit nuclear weapons.

  13. August 30, 1963

    The hotline goes live

    The hotline was not a red telephone. It was a pair of teletype machines connected by cable, so leaders could send written messages that would arrive in minutes instead of hours. The first test message was a sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet: “The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog’s back 1234567890.”
